specAnchors.text: understand, in terms of the collision theory, the effect of changes in concentration, temperature, pressure and surface area on the rate of a chemical reaction

primer.text: Reactions are collision stories: particles must meet often enough, hard enough, and facing the right way. This note builds the collision trio - frequency, energy and activation hurdle - and shows how concentration, pressure, temperature and surface area each rewrite the crash statistics.

modules.title: Successful collisions and the rate trio
modules.opening: Reacting particles crash together constantly, yet only a few crashes make products. Collision theory splits those crashes by frequency, by energy, and by the activation hurdle, and rate ends up counting the successful collisions per unit time.
keyPoints: Rate of reaction depends on collision frequency, collision energy, and the activation energy.
Rate ultimately measures the number of successful or effective collisions per unit time.
A successful collision needs the correct orientation and sufficient energy for bonds to break and new bonds to form.
Unsuccessful collisions bounce the particles apart without reaction.

low.restatement: Particles must meet (frequency), meet hard enough (energy) and meet facing the right way (orientation) for a reaction; everything else is a bounce.
low.analogy: Darts hitting a board: you must throw often, throw hard, and aim - missing any one means no score.
low.examPointer: When asked why a condition changes rate, always end at 'more frequent successful collisions per unit time'.

medium.restatement: Only collisions that combine adequate kinetic energy with productive geometry convert reactant bonds into product bonds; the rate is a census of those effective impacts, not of all impacts.
medium.analogy: Two key-and-lock attempts per second can both fail if the key is soft or turned the wrong way; only a hard, correctly turned turn opens the lock.
medium.examPointer: Distinguish 'collision frequency' (how often) from 'successful collisions' (how often AND productive) - conflating them loses the analysis mark.

modules.title: Controlling collision frequency
modules.opening: Four levers move collision frequency: concentration, pressure, temperature and particle size. But frequency alone is not the whole story - each collision must also carry enough energy, which is where most pairs fail.
keyPoints: Collision frequency counts the collisions between reactant particles in each unit of time.
Raising concentration, pressure, temperature or surface area all raise collision frequency.
Higher concentration or pressure packs more particles into the same space for more frequent meetings.
Not every collision succeeds: most pairs lack the energy to break the necessary bonds.

low.restatement: More particles in less space, faster-moving particles, or more exposed surface all raise the meeting rate; but only collisions with sufficient energy can react.
low.analogy: A busy crossroads: more traffic means more encounters, yet only encounters with enough momentum to unlock the gate lead anywhere.
low.examPointer: Pair each condition with its mechanism: concentration/pressure = more particles per volume; temperature = more kinetic energy; surface area = more exposed particles.

medium.restatement: Frequency is a counting problem - collisions per second - while success is an energy problem per collision. Temperature is the one lever that raises both counts at once: more collisions and a bigger energetic share of them.
medium.analogy: Speeding up a queue raises the number of handshakes per minute, but only firm grips (energetic collisions) conclude deals.
medium.examPointer: Do not claim higher concentration raises collision energy - it only raises collision frequency.

modules.title: Activation energy and reaction profiles
modules.opening: Every reaction charges a toll: the activation energy, the minimum energy a collision must carry before bonds will reorganise. Exothermic profiles show a low hill; endothermic ones a taller climb, because reactants start below their products.
keyPoints: The activation energy Ea is the minimum energy reactant particles need before reaction can occur.
Exothermic reactants start above their products, leaving a relatively small barrier to climb.
Endothermic reactants start below their products, so the barrier to climb is relatively larger.
Even correctly oriented collisions fail if their energy is below Ea.

low.restatement: The energy hill between reactants and products is the activation energy; exothermic reactants sit high and pay a small toll, endothermic reactants sit low and pay a larger one.
low.analogy: A summit between two valleys: walking downhill-to-downhill is an easy climb; climbing from a low valley to a high one is a longer haul.
low.examPointer: On profiles, always mark Ea as the vertical gap from reactants to the curve's peak, and label the exothermic/endothermic starting levels.

medium.restatement: Kinetic energy distributions explain the toll: only the tail of particles beyond Ea can react regardless of orientation. Endothermic reactions pay the toll plus the net energy gain, which is why their Ea is comparatively larger.
medium.analogy: A theme-park ride with a height bar: only riders taller than the bar (energy above Ea) get through, however perfectly they queue (orientation).
medium.examPointer: Quote 'minimum energy' verbatim in Ea definitions and connect relative profile heights to exothermic versus endothermic classification.

glossary.definition: The number of collisions between reactant particles per unit time in the system.
A collision with the correct orientation and at least the activation energy, producing reaction.
The minimum energy a collision must carry before reactant bonds can break and products form.
